pages.name: Fit a capacitor
pages.text: You know the fix for a poor power factor: a capacitor in parallel. This is how much, and what it does. Lesson 8's motor on 230 V mains draws 10 A while its wattmeter reads 1.6 kW. Its triangle: P = 1600 W along the floor, Q_L = 1652 var upright and S = 2300 VA, a power factor of 0.70, lagging. Now a capacitor is wired across the motor's terminals. Its current leads where the motor's lags, so its vars, Q_C, point down from the tip of Q_L. The supply sees only what is left: at 500 var, an upright of 1152 var, S = 1972 VA and 8.57 A in the cable. This is [[power factor correction]].

pages.name: The wattmeter
pages.task: The capacitor is fitted, at 500 var. What does the motor's wattmeter read now?
pages.why: The capacitor sits beside the motor, not in its path, so the motor still has 230 V across it, still draws 10 A and still takes 1600 W. A capacitor's power wave averages zero, as in lesson 8, so it takes no true power either. Only what the supply sends changes: the floor stays put while the upright shrinks.

pages.name: Cancel the upright
pages.text: The slider is yours now, up to the motor's whole 1652 var. As Q_C grows, its arrow eats into the upright, so the supply's upright, Q_L − Q_C, shrinks. S shortens, the angle closes and the cable's current falls, while P stays at 1600 W. At 1000 var the upright is 652 var, S is 1728 VA, the power factor is 0.93 and the cable carries 7.51 A.

pages.name: Power factor 1
pages.task: How many vars must the capacitor supply for a power factor of 1?
pages.why: A power factor of 1 means S lies along the floor, so the supply's upright, Q_L − Q_C, must be zero: Q_C = Q_L = 1652 var. Then S = 1600 VA and the cable carries 1600 ÷ 230 = 6.96 A instead of 10 A. Its heat goes with the current squared, (6.96 ÷ 10)² = 0.48 of what it was. 700 var is the gap between 2300 VA and 1600 W, which is not a side of the triangle. 2300 var would cancel the long side, but the floor, the watts, stays.

pages.name: The loop
pages.text: Where has the current gone? Split the motor's 10 A as lesson 8 did: an in-step part, 10 × cos 45.9° = 6.96 A, and a quarter-cycle part, 10 × sin 45.9° = 7.18 A, a quarter cycle behind the voltage. The capacitor's 1652 ÷ 230 = 7.18 A is a quarter cycle ahead. Half a cycle apart, one flows in as the other flows out, so that 7.18 A runs round the short loop between the capacitor and the motor. The supply cable carries only the in-step 6.96 A.

pages.name: The supply cable
pages.task: With the capacitor at 1652 var, the motor draws 10 A and the capacitor 7.18 A. What does the supply cable carry?
pages.why: Currents out of step add as arrows. The motor's 10 A is 6.96 A in step plus 7.18 A a quarter cycle behind. The capacitor's 7.18 A is a quarter cycle ahead, so it cancels that part exactly and leaves the in-step 6.96 A, the arrow that closes the other two along the floor. 2.82 A takes 7.18 from 10 as plain numbers, but the capacitor cancels only the quarter-cycle part. 17.18 A adds them, but they are half a cycle apart. The triangle above draws vars, where a coil's point up by convention; these arrows draw the currents themselves, measured from the voltage, where behind is down. So the capacitor's points down in one and up in the other.

pages.name: Sizing
pages.text: To size the capacitor, read three rows off the triangle. Its vars: Q_C = Q before − Q after, where Q before is the motor's Q_L and Q after is the supply's upright you want left. It has the full 230 V across it, so its current is V ÷ X_C and its vars are V² ÷ X_C, which turns round to X_C = V² ÷ Q_C. Then lesson 5's rule turned round gives C = 1 ÷ (2πf X_C), at 50 Hz. For a power factor of 1 here, that is 32.0 Ω, about 99 µF. Set the slider and the rows follow.

pages.name: A target of 0.95
pages.task: An example target: a power factor of 0.95. How many vars must the capacitor supply?
pages.why: The angle whose cosine is 0.95 is 18.2°, so the vars left are Q after = P × tan 18.2° = 1600 × 0.329 = 526 var. The capacitor supplies the rest: 1652 − 526 = 1126 var. That needs X_C = 230² ÷ 1126 = 47.0 Ω, about 68 µF, and leaves 1600 ÷ (230 × 0.95) = 7.32 A in the cable. 1570 var is 0.95 of the motor's vars, but the power factor is a ratio of the triangle's sides, not a share of the vars. 526 var is what stays.

pages.name: Too far
pages.text: Now the slider goes up to 3400 var. Past 1652 var the down arrow overshoots the floor and the triangle swings below it: the power factor is now leading. The capacitor's current has outgrown the motor's quarter-cycle part, so the difference comes along the supply cable, and the cable's current grows again, in red. At 2500 var the upright is −848 var, S is 1811 VA, the power factor is 0.88, leading, and the cable carries 7.87 A. Adding more than the load's own vars is [[over-correction]].

pages.name: Twice the capacitor
pages.task: To be sure, someone fits twice the capacitor: 3304 var. What does the supply cable carry?
pages.why: Q_C now outgrows Q_L by 1652 var, so the upright points 1652 var down: the motor's own triangle, flipped below the floor. S is back to 2300 VA, so the cable carries 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A again, at a power factor of 0.70, now leading. The capacitor's spare vars come along the cable, just as the motor's did. 6.96 A would need the upright at zero. Nearly 0 A forgets the in-step 6.96 A, which does the work.

pages.name: Mixed: a compressor
pages.task: Mixed. A compressor motor takes 3 kW and 5 kVA on 230 V, so 21.7 A. Which capacitor corrects it fully, and what current is left?
pages.why: Its vars are the upright: √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 kvar, so the capacitor supplies 4 kvar. The cable then carries only the watts' share: 3000 ÷ 230 = 13.0 A. The capacitor itself is X_C = 230² ÷ 4000 = 13.2 Ω, and C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 13.2), about 240 µF. 2 kvar takes 3 from 5, which is not a side of the triangle. 4.3 A takes the capacitor's 17.4 A from 21.7 A as plain numbers, but it cancels only the quarter-cycle part.

pages.name: Mixed: where to fit it
pages.task: Mixed. The first motor sits 20 m from its distribution board. Where does the capacitor relieve the most cable?
pages.why: The capacitor's 7.18 A runs round the loop between the capacitor and the motor. Across the motor's terminals that loop is short, so the whole 20 m run from the board carries only the in-step 6.96 A. At the board, the loop is the 20 m run itself, so the run still carries the motor's full 10 A. The triangle at the supply is the same either way, but the cable inside the loop is not relieved.
